Suspected bulk orders of large quantities of second-hand books have led many booksellers to believe the volumes are being purchased on behalf of AI companies, to be scanned and used as training material without the authors' consent or any payment being made.

An AirTag hidden inside a rare book that was part of a bulk order was eventually traced to an Amazon AI training facility, seemingly confirming the theory…

Booksellers specialising in second-hand volumes usually only receive orders for individual titles or small related batches. However, over the past period, many booksellers have reported receiving bulk orders for enormous quantities of second-hand books, with seemingly no connection between the titles.

It is suspected these books are being purchased by AI companies, which strip the spines and use high-speed scanners to ingest the text, feeding it into AI systems as training material.

Not only is this done without the authors' consent, it is also done without any payment being made for the use of their work — it is unethical at the very least, but until now there has been no concrete evidence proving it is happening. A 404 Media investigation appears to have changed that.

The investigation is behind a paywall, but TNW reports on the findings, noting the tracking device used was an AirTag, and that employees at the facility confirmed the activities being carried out there.

Second-hand books are particularly valuable because works published after 2022 may contain content written or edited by AI systems; in other words, the training process may be using AI-generated output to train AI. While publishing contracts universally explicitly prohibit authors from using AI-generated content, it is likely some still turn a blind eye. As for self-published books, there is currently no effective regulation at all.

Part of the problem is that intellectual property law has yet to catch up with this kind of operation. While it may be illegal in the UK, a 2025 ruling in the US deemed it lawful on the grounds of 'transformative' use of copyrighted works.
